news.Title: Warren Buffet’s Stock Portfolio: Top 5 Picks
news.Content: Warren Buffett no longer runs the conglomerate he built over six decades, but his fingerprints are still on nearly everything it owns. He handed the chief executive role to Greg Abel at the end of 2025, and Abel took over at the start of 2026. On September 18, Buffett, 96, stepped down as chairman, a post he had held since 1970. His son Howard Buffett now chairs the board, while Buffett stays on as chairman emeritus and a director. Abel acknowledged the weight of the handoff in his first shareholder letter on February 28. "Warren is obviously a very hard act to follow," he wrote. He also promised that Berkshire would not retreat from investing and called its huge cash pile dry powder. Abel Starts Putting Berkshire's Cash to Work The cash is moving. Berkshire reported on October 31 that it had stepped up its buybacks, and Abel has shown he will not simply copy his mentor. He bought homebuilder Taylor Morrison in July, took a stake in Italian software company Bending Spoons, and has been trimming some of Buffett's older favorites while adding new names to the portfolio. Buffett, meanwhile, stays visible, and his focus has turned from running the company to protecting its culture and giving his wealth away. He still writes the annual letters that investors read for his plain-spoken lessons, and his old rule of being greedy when others are fearful comes up whenever markets wobble. Readers who like to follow the Oracle of Omaha can browse our list of Warren Buffett stocks with upside potential for more ideas. A Portfolio Built on Buffett's Picks and Abel's Moves Even after the handoff, the portfolio still reads like Buffett's. The biggest positions are long-held companies with strong brands and loyal customers, the kind of businesses he has favored for decades, and Abel has largely left them alone. Berkshire's latest 13F filing, made on November 16, shows the pattern of a successor who respects the inheritance but is not afraid to make changes. Buffett keeps giving his own stake away. On November 16, he converted 6,150 Class A shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares for four family foundations, a gift worth about $5.5 billion. "All my Berkshire shares will be donated to the four foundations, with the goal of growing the grants each year," he wrote in his Thanksgiving letter. Those who want to see how one of his disciples invests can look at the AI stocks in a Buffett disciple's Baby Berkshire portfolio . We shared the expanded list of Warren Buffet's Stock Portfolio: Top 10 Picks here . Click the image below to watch our video covering the top 5 stocks. Story Continues Our Methodology For this article, we sifted through Berkshire Hathaway's 13F filings for Q3 2026 and ranked its top 10 stock holdings in ascending order of their stake value. At Insider Monkey, we are obsessed with what hedge funds do. The reason is simple: our research has shown that we can outperform the market by imitating the top stock picks of the best hedge funds. Insider Monkey's quarterly newsletter strategy selects 14 small-cap and large-cap stocks every quarter and has returned 612% since May 2014, beating its benchmark by 375 percentage points ( see more details here ). Warren Buffet's Stock Portfolio: Top 5 Picks 5. Bank of America (NYSE:BAC) Stake Value: $24.81 billion Bank of America serves consumers, businesses, and large corporations through retail banking, wealth management, and trading. Berkshire Hathaway owns 455,860,908 shares, which make up 8.16% of its reported 13F portfolio. Buffett stepped in during 2011 with $5 billion in preferred stock and warrants to buy shares at $7.14, a crisis-era bet that later paid off handsomely. He praised Chief Executive Officer Brian Moynihan for rebuilding a damaged bank. Investors like its scale, its low-cost deposit base, and its buybacks, which have shrunk the share count by nearly a third in a decade. Its status as one of the largest global banks also helps when regional banks come under stress. Berkshire has been selling lately, though, and it trimmed the position again in the third quarter. UBS reiterated its Buy rating on Bank of America and its $62 target on November 11 after meeting with Moynihan. In the third quarter ended September 30, 2026, net income was $6.9 billion, or $0.91 per share, including a $1.2 billion regulatory settlement charge. Excluding the charge, earnings were $1.08 per share. Our look at whether its wealth business is worth more than the headline bank suggests makes the bull case. 4. Alphabet Class A (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Stake Value: $27.11 billion Berkshire Hathaway owns 78,791,167 Class A shares of Alphabet, which make up 8.91% of its reported 13F portfolio. The position, Berkshire's biggest bet on the company, grew sharply in 2026 as Abel added shares. Alphabet is the parent of Google Services, Google Cloud, and the Other Bets ventures. Buffett once admitted he should have bought Google years earlier, and Berkshire finally started buying in the third quarter of 2025. Bulls say the stock pairs a dominant core business with multiple ways to profit from AI. They also like its data advantage and a valuation that makes it the cheapest of the Magnificent Seven by price-to-earnings ratio. Wells Fargo cut its price target on Alphabet to $365 from $371 on November 2 but kept an Overweight rating, as it sees Search growth slowing while it raised its Cloud estimates by 7%. Alphabet's third quarter ended September 30, 2026, was strong. Revenue rose 25% to $127.6 billion, and operating income jumped 30%. Cloud operating income rose to $11.12 billion from $3.59 billion. We looked at what Waymo could be worth to Alphabet in a separate piece. 3. Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO) Stake Value: $34.43 billion Coca-Cola sells soft drinks, juices, sports drinks, and water in more than 200 countries and territories. Berkshire Hathaway owns 400,000,000 shares, which make up 11.32% of its reported 13F portfolio. Buffett started buying in 1988 and has joked that he is one-fourth Coca-Cola, and Abel has kept the position intact. It is the business Buffett loves most: a brand people recognize everywhere, an asset-light model, and the power to raise prices without losing customers. Investors also point to its grip on shelf space and a dividend raised for 64 straight years, which pays Berkshire hundreds of millions of dollars a year. TD Cowen named Coca-Cola its top pick for 2027 on November 17, rated Coca-Cola a Buy, and raised its price target to $112 from $104. In the third quarter ended October 2, 2026, unit case volume grew 5%, and net revenues rose 7% to $13.4 billion. Comparable EPS rose 11% to $0.91, and management raised its full-year guidance. We asked whether the stock can hold its price in our piece on whether Coca-Cola can support 28 times earnings . 2. American Express (NYSE:AXP) Stake Value: $46.10 billion American Express issues premium charge and credit cards and runs the payment network behind them. Berkshire Hathaway owns 151,610,700 shares, which make up 15.16% of its reported 13F portfolio, and it has held the stock since 1991 without selling a share. "You can't create another American Express," Buffett told Bloomberg in a 2022 interview. The appeal is the brand's premium image, a closed-loop network that earns both fees and interest, and wealthier customers who keep spending through downturns. Buybacks have cut the share count by about 27% in a decade, and the company raised its dividend 16% this year. UBS kept its Hold rating on American Express on November 2 and raised its price target to $346 from $345. In the third quarter ended September 30, 2026, revenue rose 9% to $20.06 billion, and net income jumped 28% to $3.71 billion. Adjusted earnings per share rose 13% to $4.68, and the company raised full-year guidance to $18.30 to $18.60 per share. Our look at whether young cardholders could become American Express's most valuable customers covers the next generation. 1. Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) Stake Value: $75.90 billion Apple designs and sells iPhones, Macs, iPads, wearables, and services. Berkshire Hathaway owns 227,917,808 shares, which make up 24.95% of its reported 13F portfolio and make Apple its largest holding. Buffett has said he did not buy Apple as a tech stock. "Apple has an extraordinary consumer franchise," he told CNBC. He liked the ecosystem that keeps users loyal, the steady buybacks, and the strong cash flow. Abel stopped the selling that Buffett had overseen for almost two years. Investors today also like that Apple is not spending heavily on AI, which has made it a haven, while its Services business carries higher margins. Bernstein raised its price target on Apple to $380 from $370 on November 4 and kept an Outperform rating. On November 11, China Renaissance upgraded Apple to Buy from Hold with a $425 target. Both followed a fiscal fourth quarter ended September 26, 2026, when revenue rose 12% to a September-quarter record of $114.5 billion and diluted EPS rose 14% to $2.10. For more on the stock, see what Ken Fisher and Jim Cramer like about Apple . While we acknowledge the risk and potential of AAPL as an investment, we believe certain AI infrastructure stocks offer far stronger long-term potential at a much more attractive entry point. If you are looking for an AI stock more promising than AAPL that operates as a critical AI tollbooth and stands as the most important company in the world, check out our report about this must-own AI stock . news.Title: After Plummeting 62% This Year, Could Buying Intel Stock Today Set You Up for Life?
news.Content:
Few stocks in the semiconductor sector have experienced a more dramatic fall this year than Intel (NASDAQ:INTC). Since reaching a peak closing price of nearly $141 per share in June, the stock has lost 62% of its value.

This has attracted bargain hunters who perceived Intel as a stock to own, and some may wonder whether Intel can set investors for life. Although Intel could beat the market over time, investors should not assume that a modest investment in the stock will bring financial independence. Here's why.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

The reemergence of Intel

The prospect for Intel's return to prominence has dramatically improved under Lip-Bu Tan. The former Cadence Design Systems CEO has begun leveraging Intel's existing competitive advantages to compete in today's semiconductor industry .

In short, Tan is forging ahead where the previous Intel CEO, Pat Gelsinger, fell short. Intel has finally succeeded with its longtime plan to master advanced chip production with its 18A manufacturing process node.

This has allowed it to produce chips smaller than 2nm in the U.S., making it more competitive with the industry's dominant manufacturer, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC). That move could signal a revival in U.S. chip manufacturing.

Moreover, Fortune Business Insights forecasts that the artificial intelligence (AI) chip market will grow at a 30% compound annual rate through 2034, positioning Intel in a lucrative growth market.

Additionally, during Gelsinger's tenure, Intel opened its production capacity to third-party manufacturers. The foundry continues to flourish, attracting business from companies like Microsoft and Amazon 's AWS. It has also made a deal with Tesla, with its upcoming 14A process node slated for production beginning in the second half of 2027.

Intel's growth prospects

Although these improvements could make Intel a market-beating stock, the law of large numbers hampers Intel's ability to make small investors wealthy.

When investors read stories about $5,000 investments turning into millions, that is usually a case of a small- or mid-cap stock eventually becoming one of America's largest companies.

Unfortunately for investors who want Intel to set them up for life, Intel remained in large-cap territory even at the height of its more recent troubles.

Story Continues

Also, despite its recent decline, its market capitalization is just over $290 billion. That places it among the 50 largest companies trading on U.S. markets today. Doubling that four times would take Intel's market value close to that of today's market cap leader, Apple , at $5.2 trillion. Still, while doubling four times is an impressive return, it would take a $5,000 investment to about $80,000, not enough to set one up for life.

Furthermore, despite optimism about its future, analysts project 17% revenue growth this year, then 12% in 2027. That is lower than the aforementioned CAGR, suggesting it may take some time for Intel's AI-driven growth to reach its full potential.

Achieving that potential will likely take time, as competing in these markets requires considerable capital expenditures (capex). Over the trailing 12 months alone, Intel's capex was $16 billion.

Although free cash flow remains positive for now, such spending likely contributed to Intel's Q3 warnings about negative free cash flow in future quarters.

Amid the considerable demand for AI chips, Intel could overcome these challenges. Moreover, even though its P/E ratio reflects profitability that is too low to serve as a meaningful valuation measure, the forward P/E ratio of 37 suggests Intel stock now trades at a reasonable price.

Nonetheless, even if Intel ultimately brings investors closer to being set for life, its current financial condition indicates the process will take longer.

Intel takeaways

Given Intel's massive size, the company's stock is unlikely to set a small investor up for life. Still, it offers the possibility of making considerable progress toward that goal -- if one has patience.

Intel's technical breakthroughs appear to have given TSMC a viable competitor and a path to again capitalize on the cutting edge of semiconductor technology.

Unfortunately for investors, Intel's market cap indicates it has grown too large to set up a small investor for life.

Investors can now buy Intel at an increasingly attractive valuation, and amid its growth opportunities, Intel's stock price could be much higher after one year. However, investors who buy this stock should not expect an investment in Intel alone to make them financially independent.

news.Title: Here's How Much Cash Anthropic Has After Its IPO, and Why It Could Be the Most Important Number for Investors to Know
news.Content:
Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) just completed the largest IPO on record, and it now has an enormous amount of money in the bank. On Friday, the company said its underwriters had exercised their option to buy an additional 147 million shares at the $83 IPO price, bringing the total raised in the offering to $93.5 billion. Including a $26 billion private placement with a group of tech companies, Anthropic's gross proceeds came to $119.5 billion.

The stock has had a bumpy start. Shares opened at $111.50 on Thursday, closed at $97.17, and then fell further on Friday amid a broad tech sell-off. It's easy to get caught up in daily price swings, but for long-term investors, I'd argue that Anthropic's cash pile is one of the most important things to understand about the company right now. Here's why.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

How much cash does Anthropic have now?

Anthropic hasn't reported a post-IPO balance sheet yet, so we'll need to estimate. As of Sept. 30, the company had about $132 billion in cash and investments.

Next, we need to add the IPO money . Anthropic won't keep all $119.5 billion, since the underwriters take a cut and a deal this size comes with other expenses. Based on the estimates in Anthropic's prospectus, fees and expenses should amount to a little over 1% of the IPO proceeds, and the private placement didn't include an underwriting discount. That leaves net proceeds of roughly $118 billion.

Put it all together, and Anthropic likely has about $250 billion in cash and short-term investments right now. It also has about $14.8 billion available on its revolving credit line, which brings its total liquidity to roughly $265 billion.

Of course, this is a rough estimate. Anthropic has been generating and spending cash since the end of September, and we won't see the official figure until the company reports its fourth-quarter results.

Why Anthropic needs so much cash

Training and running frontier AI models takes a staggering amount of computing power, and Anthropic has about $900 billion of compute and infrastructure commitments. These include cloud contracts with Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet 's Google (NASDAQ:GOOGL)(NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), equipment leases with Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and leases on data centers that haven't been built yet. On top of that, Anthropic expects to pay an estimated $150 billion to $175 billion under arrangements without fixed dollar amounts, including additional Google chip capacity scheduled for delivery between 2028 and 2031.

Story Continues

That's a massive figure for a company with about $81 billion of run rate revenue, and it's the main reason some investors are nervous about the stock. Most of these commitments can't be canceled, so Anthropic will owe much of the money whether or not customer demand keeps up.

The near-term commitments are well covered

While it's easy to focus on the $900 billion figure, the good news is that these commitments are spread out over a long period. The bills coming due soon are a small fraction of the total.

Anthropic expects about $70.7 billion of its commitments to come due in the 12 months following Sept. 30. The estimated $250 billion cash pile covers that amount about 3.5 times over, without counting a single dollar of new cash flow. And the business also generated about $6.6 billion of operating cash flow in the first nine months of 2026.

Looking further out, Anthropic has said it expects about $447.5 billion of its commitments to be incurred by the end of 2030. The company's current cash pile alone could cover more than half of that, before counting any cash its operations generate over the next four years. About $186 billion of the total also comes with termination rights or depends on certain conditions being met, which gives Anthropic some degree of flexibility if demand falls short of its plans.

What could go wrong

Of course, $250 billion can go faster than you might think at this scale, and there's no guarantee that Anthropic will be able to fund all of its commitments without posting big losses along the way.

The key risk is a mismatch between revenue and costs. Most of Anthropic's revenue is consumption-based, meaning customers pay for what they use and can cut back at any time, while most of its compute commitments are locked in.

With revenue growth of more than 1,100% in the third quarter, Anthropic's revenue will slow down from here. But if it slows faster than expected, the commitments later this decade could become a heavy burden. Anthropic has also said its longer-term funding will depend on revenue growth, operating cash flow, and access to additional capital, so another capital raise down the road isn't out of the question.

Why this matters for investors

Having said all that, the IPO gave Anthropic something valuable: time to grow. With an estimated $250 billion in the bank, the company can meet its near-term obligations several times over and keep investing in new models without needing to raise money in a volatile market for years. That should reduce the risk of a dilutive capital raise at a bad time, which is one of the biggest dangers for any fast-growing company with heavy spending commitments.

The question for Anthropic stock investors is whether revenue keeps growing fast enough to cover the larger bills coming later this decade. When Anthropic reports fourth-quarter results, I'll be watching its cash balance, its operating cash flow, and any changes to its compute commitments closely. If the cash pile holds up and revenue keeps climbing, the bear case about Anthropic's spending will look a lot less convincing.

news.Title: Prediction: Nvidia Stock Will Be Worth This Much in 1 Year
news.Content:
On Nov. 12, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) founder and chief executive officer Jensen Huang resigned from his post after a series of extramarital affairs (including one with an alleged Chinese spy) came to light. To make matters worse, the U.S. government is now investigating some of the company's customers in Southeast Asia to determine whether advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips were illegally forwarded to businesses in China.

Nvidia stock has plummeted by 37% from its peak amid the turmoil, and it's now trading at the cheapest valuation in a decade. However, the company just reported a blockbuster set of operating results for its fiscal 2027 third quarter (ended Oct. 25), and interim CEO Colette Kress even issued a higher revenue forecast for the upcoming 2028 fiscal year.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

As a result, while Nvidia's challenges are likely to cause further short-term volatility in its stock, I think its booming business and solid fundamentals will ultimately prevail. Here's where I predict the stock will be trading in one year.

Image source: Nvidia.

The Vera Rubin launch has been a resounding success

Nvidia has come a long way since launching its first dedicated AI graphics processing unit (GPU) for the data center, the Hopper-based H100, in 2022. It went on to release the Blackwell and Blackwell Ultra architectures in 2024 and 2025, the latter of which can deliver up to 50 times more output performance than Hopper.

But Nvidia started shipping its new Vera Rubin systems during the recent third quarter, which include the Rubin GPU, Vera central processing unit (CPU), and a series of upgraded networking components. It can deliver up to 30 times the performance of the equivalent Blackwell Ultra system, translating into a potential 97% reduction in inference token costs.

Inference tokens are the text, images, or computer code generated by an AI model in response to a prompt, so Vera Rubin could significantly reduce the cost of running AI software. This is likely to drive greater AI adoption while making data center operators more profitable, fueling further demand for Nvidia's chips.

Colette Kress said Vera Rubin achieved almost $20 billion in sales during the third quarter alone, making this the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history.

Story Continues

Nvidia's third-quarter revenue doubled

Nvidia generated a record $115.8 billion in revenue during the third quarter, a whopping 103% increase from the year-ago period. The data center segment alone accounted for $107.6 billion of that total, and it grew at an even faster pace of 110%.

Nvidia's physical AI business also deserves a mention. It develops the hardware and software technologies required to run robots, autonomous vehicles, industrial systems, and more, and its revenue more than tripled year over year during the third quarter. It's now on track to generate $25 billion in total sales for the current fiscal year (which ends on Jan. 31, 2027), so it could soon become a key source of growth for the entire company.

Kress also said Nvidia could deliver $130 billion in total revenue during the fourth quarter, exceeding Wall Street's consensus expectation of $125.1 billion. Plus, she told investors that revenue could grow by 75% during fiscal 2028, upping the company's original forecast of 70% from a few months ago.

That was a very positive surprise, and it dispels some of the speculation that Nvidia's sales will take a major hit amid any potential investigations into its dealings with customers in Southeast Asia.

Nvidia stock is trading at the cheapest valuation in a decade

Jensen Huang and Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, are expected to testify before Congress in early December, where they will be questioned about potential national security breaches involving the prohibited sale of advanced AI chips to China. It's difficult to know what will come of these hearings, but I think investors are now being compensated for the potential risks because of Nvidia's rock-bottom valuation.

Nvidia stock is trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 16.2 as I write this on Nov. 19, which is a fraction of its 10-year average of 61.1. It's also the lowest valuation in a decade.

Moreover, Wall Street still believes Nvidia will grow its earnings to $16.61 per share in fiscal 2028, placing its forward P/E ratio at just 9.1. For some perspective, that's less than half the forward P/E of the Nasdaq-100 index, which is 20.7, so Nvidia looks extremely undervalued compared to a collective of America's leading technology giants.

NVDA PE Ratio data by YCharts

As a result, I think there is room for Nvidia stock to trade significantly higher over the next 12 months, provided the company's fiscal 2028 guidance remains intact and isn't disrupted by a slowdown in AI infrastructure spending, a loss of market share, or government investigations. These are genuine risks, but Kress's decision to raise the forecast suggests the sales pipeline is robust enough to weather them.

Even if Nvidia stock doubles over the next year, it will still be cheaper than the Nasdaq-100 on a P/E basis, so I feel confident predicting a price of at least $200. But I think there is a real chance the stock reclaims its previous high of $239.

news.Title: Applied Materials vs. Nvidia: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
news.Content:
The global semiconductor industry is undergoing a massive transformation driven by the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence. Choosing between Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) requires understanding whether you want to own the tools or the chips.

Applied Materials builds the specialized equipment and software used to manufacture semiconductors, making it a foundational player in the hardware supply chain. Nvidia designs the high-performance graphics processors and systems that power modern data centers. Both companies are central to the future of technology, but they offer different risk and reward profiles for investors.

The case for Applied Materials

Applied Materials provides materials engineering solutions and specialized equipment used to manufacture semiconductors and display screens. It serves a global customer base primarily among semiconductor stocks , including manufacturers of advanced logic and memory chips. In its latest annual report, the company noted that two major customers accounted for nearly 19% and 15% of net revenue, and such customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 25, 2026, revenue reached approximately $34.4 billion, an increase of nearly 21.4% over the prior 12-month period. Net income for this time frame was roughly $10.1 billion, resulting in a healthy net margin of close to 29.3%. This expansion followed a period of steady demand for manufacturing equipment as chipmakers expanded their global production capacity.

As of its October 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was nearly 0.3. This metric measures total debt relative to shareholder equity to show how much a company relies on borrowed funds to finance its operations. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to liabilities, was approximately 2.3. In the fiscal year ended Oct. 25, 2026, free cash flow reached nearly $6.2 billion.

The case for Nvidia

Nvidia designs the high-performance graphics processors, systems, and software that define the modern artificial intelligence landscape. The company describes itself as a full-stack infrastructure provider, serving clients across data centers, gaming, and professional visualization. In its latest annual report, Nvidia disclosed that sales to one direct customer accounted for approximately 22% of revenue, while another accounted for nearly 14%, creating significant concentration risk.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 25, 2026, revenue reached nearly $361.8 billion, representing a massive 93.3% increase over the previous 12 months. Net income climbed to approximately $226.3 billion, producing a robust net margin of roughly 62.5% for the period. This exponential growth reflects the intense and sustained global demand for high-end computing hardware used in training complex AI models.

Story Continues

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.1. The current ratio was approximately 3.9. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 25, 2026, free cash flow was approximately $96.7 billion.

Risk profile comparison

Applied Materials faces significant exposure to the highly cyclical and volatile semiconductor industry. The company maintains a heavy concentration of operations in China, Taiwan, and Korea, which creates risks from changing trade policies. Furthermore, a recent $252 million settlement regarding shipments to a restricted entity highlights the ongoing risk of export control compliance.

Nvidia relies heavily on third-party foundries like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE:TSM) for production, which reduces its control over manufacturing yields. The company faces potential volatility from ongoing securities class action lawsuits and the challenges of managing transitions to new product architectures. Finally, Nvidia is in the midst of an unexpected leadership transition, which introduces its own uncertainties.

Valuation comparison

Nvidia appears cheaper based on forward P/E estimates of future profits, while Applied Materials carries a lower P/S ratio relative to sales over the past 12 months.

Which stock would I buy for 2027?

What a time to be picking stocks, am I right? The market's having a minor meltdown, but tech names in particular are taking it on the chin. Nvidia is also dealing with the sudden departure of co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang following the revelation of multiple extramarital affairs. The year-to-date chart looks grim:

AMAT data by YCharts

That said, widening our perspective out to the past 10 years, both stocks have put in strong performances, handily outpacing the S&P 500 's (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) return:

NVDA data by YCharts

I have in the past expressed my general doubts regarding Nvidia because its growth is largely tied to the AI boom. "A boom doesn't look very different from a bubble," I wrote . I don't feel differently now. Sure, Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) had a record public debut just days ago, but it gave up a lot of its first-day gains.

Applied Materials' growth and profitability can't hold a candle to Nvidia's, but I think investing in Nvidia right now may be like trying to catch a falling knife. I'd sit this one out.

news.Title: The Stock Market Just Had Its Worst Week of 2026. Here's Why Long-Term Investors Shouldn't Flinch.
news.Content:
The U.S. midterm election has ushered in some of the most stock market volatility we've seen since the start of the Iran war. In the two days following Election Day, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) experienced both its best and worst trading sessions since April 2025. The 2.7% decline for the week as a whole is also the worst in 19 months.

Since we haven't seen a week like this in a while, you might think it's rare. It isn't. If you're a long-term investor and reacted to virtually any of the trading days we've seen this month, it might be worth reconsidering just how small the move was in the bigger picture.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Even the worst week wasn't that bad

The election-week losses have helped push the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) to nearly 7% below its all-time high. But those kinds of pullbacks have actually been fairly normal over even just the past year.

In November 2025, the S&P 500 was roughly 5% below its high. It was back at a new high by December.

The beginning of 2026 saw a 9% pullback in the S&P 500 around the start of the Iran war. Again, the index reached a new high in less than a month.

The S&P 500 came close to falling 5% in June of this year. While it didn't technically hit a new high until August, it only took a few trading days to recover more than half of it.

That's three separate incidents over just the past year before what happened in November. Their relatively quick turnarounds may have made them largely forgettable. But pullbacks like this are far more common than you might think.

Quick rebounds have made selling an expensive mistake

But it's the speed of the recoveries that has made these pullbacks especially dangerous. If you saw the S&P 500 falling and decided to sell in order to protect yourself, you had almost no time to buy back in before it was too late.

And that's the biggest problem with trying to time the market. The typical outcome is you lock in the losses after selling, but you miss out on the subsequent rebound. All you've essentially done is damage your portfolio's returns .

That's why long-term investors shouldn't flinch. These kinds of 5%-10% declines in the S&P 500 are normal and should be expected when investing in equities. It's simply the price of admission to the stock market.

Story Continues

Trying to react to short-term volatility is usually a bad idea. If you're a long-term investor, riding out the ups and downs is the key to success.

news.Title: The Nasdaq Just Triggered a Correction. 1 Move I'm Making Right Now -- and 1 I'm Avoiding
news.Content:
The S&P 500 index (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) includes the 500 largest publicly traded companies in America. Its name is often interchangeable with "the stock market" because the 500 large-cap stocks in this index make up about 80% of the total U.S. stock market capitalization.

So, when "the stock market" (as in the S&P 500) loses more than 10% of its value in a month, people get nervous. As of Nov. 20, since reaching its record high on Oct. 6, the S&P 500 is down about 11.6%.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The biggest driver of this recent stock market swoon is the same reason stocks have been delivering such strong results since 2022: the artificial intelligence (AI) industry. Big-spending AI hyperscalers and innovative AI frontier labs have been buoyed by investor enthusiasm for futuristic technology that promises to boost productivity and economic growth.

But to get to that bright future, these AI companies have been spending (and borrowing) hundreds of billions of dollars. Investors are starting to balk at the high price of AI. As a result of these AI fears, the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index has fallen even further than the S&P 500. The tech sector benchmark is down about 20% since Oct. 6 -- heading into a bear market.

It's understandable to feel nervous when the stock market is falling like this, but investors need to take heart, stay calm, and have confidence in the future. If you've been investing as long as I have (or longer), you've lived through worse than this.

Here's one move I'm making with my investments right now and one I'm avoiding.

Image source: Getty Images.

One move I'm making with my investments: Buying stocks

It's easy to say and harder to do, but it's true: When stock prices are plummeting, that's when I try to just keep buying more stocks. A 10% stock market correction or a 20% (or worse) bear market is ironically the best time to buy stocks. It means stocks are "on sale."

So that's what I'm doing. I'm going to keep buying stocks in a diversified portfolio of low-cost index funds. My favorite U.S. index fund is the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (NYSEMKT:VTI) because it lets me own 3,511 U.S. stocks of all sizes and industries, not just the tech sector.

Additionally, times when the U.S. stock market is struggling can be good occasions to diversify with international stocks. I'm going to keep buying the Vanguard Total International Stock ETF (NASDAQ:VXUS) and its remarkably diversified portfolio of 8,874 stocks from dozens of other countries beyond the U.S. market.

Story Continues

Eviedence shows that corrections and bear markets are temporary. If you look at the long run of stock market history, the S&P 500 has always bounced back from even the biggest stock market crashes and economic crises.

Because I'm diversified with a portfolio of thousands of stocks from the U.S. and around the world, I believe that there's never a "bad time" to buy stocks. The stock market might keep falling for a while, even after I buy my next shares -- that's OK. I don't know which individual companies or industries will be the winners or losers -- that's fine, too. By owning these index funds, I'm betting on the stock market itself to sort out the winners for me.

Buying "all the stocks" this way lets me own a piece of the global economy's long-term upside.

One move I'm avoiding with my investments: Selling stocks

It's usually a bad idea for investors to sell stocks during a bear market. It's a little like selling a car or a house that's underwater on the loan -- it puts you in a disadvantaged position and locks in your losses.

(The only exception is if you have individual stock positions that you no longer believe in and want to sell at a loss for tax-loss harvesting purposes. That's a longer conversation to be had with a professional tax advisor.)

With a diversified portfolio of index funds that I'm holding for the long term, I'm not looking to sell anything right now. That's because I don't need the money out of my investment portfolio right now; I need it 20 or 30 years in the future. I don't need to liquidate my investment portfolio for cash. I don't need my stocks to go up today or tomorrow or next year. I need them to deliver long-term returns for the next 20 years or more.

news.Title: Here's How Much $2,500 in General Mills Stock Could Pay You in Dividends in 2027
news.Content:
General Mills (NYSE:GIS) is in the middle of a multi-year turnaround. Early operating metrics suggest the effort is gaining traction in 2026.

After years of post-pandemic price hikes pushed budget-conscious shoppers toward store brands, the Minneapolis-based food giant rolled back everyday prices across two-thirds of its North American retail portfolio. The strategy has helped narrow market-share losses in key categories. Core brands like Cheerios, Cinnamon Toast Crunch, and Lucky Charms are back to growing, while new high-protein snacks and fresh pet foods are catching on.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Conserving cash for a smarter turnaround

Of course, General Mills also broke a long-standing habit by leaving its quarterly dividend parked at $0.61 per share rather than bumping it up this past summer. Honestly, I hope the board keeps it frozen for another couple of years. When you are trying to revitalize legacy brands, absorb rising wheat and freight costs, and trim debt, hanging on to extra cash for active turnaround plays is just smart business 101.

It's OK if that brand boost and distribution revamp takes a while, as long as General Mills gets it done.

Inflationary storms never last forever

Still, history offers a useful lantern for long-term shareholders navigating an inflationary squeeze. Demand for name-brand consumer staples tends to meander during periods of acute economic stress, as households trade down to store brands and discount alternatives. In the 1970s, double-digit inflation severely tested consumer purchasing power before cooling to roughly 4% in the 1980s and lower still in subsequent decades.

Across those cycles, investors who accumulated shares of durable, brand-leading businesses with reliable dividend policies were consistently rewarded once household budgets stabilized. General Mills fits that profile, flaunting category leaders like Cheerios, Nature Valley, Pillsbury, and Blue Buffalo. These household brands are not going away.

"Lucky Charms is back to growth, and Reese's Puffs is back to growth, and Cinnamon Toast Crunch is back to growth," CEO Jeff Harmening said on the Q1 2027 earnings call in September. "And that has nothing to do with anything to do with pricing. It has to do with really good marketing and really good product news."

Story Continues

Crunching the 2027 dividend numbers

So what does that patience actually pay while you wait for the recovery? Let's run the numbers using General Mills' Nov. 19 closing price of $34.48 per share. Putting approximately $2,500 to work at that price gets you roughly 73 shares of stock.

Assuming the board holds the quarterly dividend steady at $0.61 per share throughout next year, as it did over the last year and a half, those 73 shares would generate $178.12 in dividend income during 2027 (or roughly $178). At today's prices, that's an annualized yield of nearly 7.1%.

Better yet, you aren't paying a steep price for that cash flow. At roughly 10.1 times forward earnings and 11.9 times trailing free cash flow, the stock is priced like Cheerios are going out of style. Call me biased, but my breakfast bowl disagrees.

If you believe in the staying power of these household brands, locking in a roughly 7% yield at a bargain valuation sets you up nicely for brisk total returns once the consumer storm finally passes. After rain comes sunshine, and General Mills will pay dividends in both weather patterns.

news.Title: Not Anthropic. Not SpaceX. This Is the AI Stock to Buy for the Long Term
news.Content:
The Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) initial public offering (IPO) this week reinforced the view that, despite recent turbulence related to developments at Nvidia , investment in artificial intelligence (AI) remains in high-growth mode. That's not in doubt; still, the key question for retail investors is how to find the best-value way to invest in it. Companies like the AI lab and Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX), with its AI infrastructure, rocket launch, and connectivity businesses, appear attractive on this basis. Still, I think there's another company that's a better buy on a risk-adjusted basis: On Semiconductor (NASDAQ:ON).

What you need to believe in to buy AI-related stocks

To buy into the investment theme, you need to believe that the use of AI applications will continue to grow, spurring growth for AI enterprises like Anthropic and, in turn, demand for SpaceX's data center infrastructure. While these assumptions about the outlook for end demand seem entirely feasible, the reality is that both companies are engaged in a fiercely competitive, highly capital-intensive arms race.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

In Anthropic's case, it needs to continually and heavily invest in leasing compute capacity from infrastructure services (including those from SpaceX) to compete for frontier model supremacy with its rivals -- a group that actually includes SpaceX. Anthropic has already made over $900 billion in spending commitments, including $120.5 billion in an agreement with SpaceX.

In turn, compute providers like SpaceX and the well-known hyperscalers are having to make massive investments into new data center capacity to meet their contractual obligations. These investments are not risk-free. In SpaceX's case in particular, there are serious questions about how quickly its planned orbital data center satellites will depreciate . SpaceX also faces launch risk every time it attempts to send any cargo into space, and if it merges with Tesla , the company will be part of a much larger and more complex business.

All told, if there's any slowdown in demand for AI applications, both Anthropic and SpaceX are likely to suffer disproportionately.

Why On Semiconductor is a better buy

The power and sensing chip company is largely a play on the increasing power density, not only in its core automotive and industrial end markets, but also in its fast-growing data center business. The company is best known for power control chips and sensing technology that are used in electric vehicles (EVs), as well as myriad industrial applications ranging from EV charging and industrial automation to renewable energy and consumer electronics.

Story Continues

As an investment, On Semiconductor is not without risk. Its core automotive business is exposed to the cyclicality of the EV market; the power semiconductor market is competitive, and there's execution risk around its recent AI-related acquisitions. However, the diversity of its end markets means it doesn't face the same degree of existential risk as companies like Anthropic and SpaceX do from frontier model competition and capital-intensive investments.

On Semiconductor's growth prospects

In contrast to many AI-related companies, On Semiconductor is highly cash-generative, with Wall Street analysts targeting $2 billion in free cash flow (FCF) for 2027 and $2.3 billion for 2028, according to Visible Alpha. Based on its current market cap of $25.1 billion, the stock would be trading at 12.6 times FCF in 2027 and 10.9 times FCF in 2028.

Those are highly attractive valuations for any company whose management is targeting 30% annual operating income growth from 2026 to 2030. In that period, its data center revenue growth is expected to grow at a 50% annual rate.

On top of all of this, On Semiconductor's power and sensing solutions are set to become a key feature of physical AI solutions (such as robots, EVs, drones, and industrial machines) over the long term. As more physical AI products are developed, there will be an increasing need for edge power density. For example, robots can't wait a few seconds for calculations in the cloud; they need to process sensory inputs in real time, which requires power and sensing chips.

As such, the company has significant exposure to a major AI investment theme, but doesn't trade at a nosebleed valuation, and doesn't carry the kind of downside risk inherent in other pure-play AI stocks.

news.Title: CME vs. Robinhood Markets: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
news.Content:
Market volatility often creates opportunities for the platforms that facilitate trading. Deciding between CME Group (NASDAQ:CME) and Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ:HOOD) involves weighing the stability of an institutional giant against a fast-growing retail disruptor.

CME Group provides the essential infrastructure for global derivatives trading, offering unmatched liquidity to professional investors. Robinhood Markets has transitioned from a simple trading app to a diversified financial services provider for the modern retail investor. Both companies are positioned to benefit from increased market activity but offer different paths for shareholders.

The case for CME

CME Group operates the world's most diverse derivatives marketplace, offering contracts across interest rates, equities, and commodities in 200 countries. Key partnerships include a 10-year agreement with Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and a prediction market joint venture with Flutter Entertainment (NYSE:FLUT). Because one company accounted for roughly 12% of clearing and transaction fees in its latest report, this customer concentration adds a layer of risk.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $7 billion, an increase of approximately 9% over the prior period. During this time, net income was roughly $4.4 billion as the company benefited from increased trading volumes. CME maintains a high net margin of approximately 63.1%, highlighting its strength among financial stocks .

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.1. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity, indicating the company uses very little borrowed money to fund its operations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $4.2 billion, reflecting strong cash conversion from its earnings.

The case for Robinhood Markets

Robinhood Markets provides retail brokerage, advisory, and digital banking services to millions of funded customers. Its platform supports trading in traditional assets as well as Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC). It also operates a joint venture with Susquehanna International Group to run an independent futures exchange and clearinghouse.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $5.1 billion, fueled by revenue growth of approximately 21.1%. The company reported net income of close to $2 billion for the same period, reflecting success in scaling its subscription services and interest-earning assets. Its net margin for this time frame was roughly 39%.

Story Continues

As of Robinhood's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 1.3. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached nearly $1.6 billion, showing the company's ability to generate cash while expanding.

Risk profile comparison

CME Group faces intense competition from other global exchanges like Intercontinental Exchange (NYSE:ICE) and Nasdaq (NASDAQ:NDAQ). The company is also subject to regulatory and legislative changes that could impact its clearinghouse and transaction structures. Furthermore, the company manages operational risks related to third-party data centers, highlighted by a cooling failure in November 2025. Cybersecurity threats targeting financial infrastructure also remain a persistent risk for the exchange operator.

Robinhood Markets is sensitive to regulatory scrutiny regarding payment for order flow, which accounts for a substantial portion of its revenue. It competes with established brokerages like Charles Schwab (NYSE:SCHW) and fintech rivals that may have greater capital and brand recognition. The company also depends on a limited number of liquidity providers, such as Virtu Financial (NYSE:VIRT), to execute its trades. Additionally, legal challenges regarding the offering of event contracts could impact Robinhood's future product road map.

Valuation comparison

Robinhood Markets is cheaper by its P/S ratio, which measures market cap against sales over the past 12 months, while CME Group has a lower forward P/E.

Which stock would I buy for 2027?

It's a little hard to pick one over the other because of the current macro environment. Specifically, the market is, as the youths say, crashing out. Robinhood stock is less than a dollar away from its 52-week low. I mean, this year-to-date chart is brutal:

CME data by YCharts

Its stock is also a lot more volatile than CME Group's. Robinhood has seen stronger revenue growth recently, but CME posts a consistently higher profit margin. (This chart's a little wonky because Robinhood didn't go public until 2021.)

CME Profit Margin data by YCharts

In addition to CME's better profitability, I like that it pays a modest dividend yielding about 1.7%.

I think in a somewhat unsettled market like the one we're currently experiencing, a mature, established operator looks like a more attractive stock. Some investors may prefer growth over consistency, in which case, Robinhood may be more appealing. But for me, CME Group gets my vote for 2027 and beyond.

news.Title: Prediction: This Will Be Micron’s Stock Price by the End of 2028
news.Content:
Few companies have seen their earnings soar amid the artificial intelligence boom like Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU). The memory chipmaker has benefited from a spike in demand for its chips, even as it and its competitors take years to ramp up new supply capacity. The result is eye-popping profit margins and a stock price that's gone parabolic.

The stock trades for about $690 per share as of this writing, an impressive 201% gain over the past year and a 598% gain over the past 18 months. Even so, the stock is about 43% off its all-time high reached over the summer.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But as the saying goes, "Past results are not indicative of future returns." Future potential investors need to consider what they can expect from Micron and what that means for the stock price. Here's my prediction for Micron's stock price by the end of 2028.

Image source: Getty Images.

How much higher can Micron stock climb?

Micron's earnings growth is directly tied to its ability to charge extremely high prices for memory, specifically high bandwidth memory (HBM), which gets packaged with GPUs and AI accelerators for AI training and inference.

As a result, Micron's gross margin has climbed to an astonishing 87%. But that pricing isn't indicative of a competitive moat, as many high-gross-margin businesses exhibit. Note that rival chipmaker SK Hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) produced a gross margin of 86% in its most recent quarter, practically on par with Micron.

The margin strength stems from the supply/demand imbalance. Micron said supply constraints will be even tighter in 2027 and 2028 than they were in 2026 in its fourth-quarter earnings presentation. That suggests prices could keep climbing through 2028.

SK Hynix suggested that demand could outpace supply through 2030. But just because demand remains higher than supply doesn't mean prices will keep climbing. Demand has to grow faster than supply.

So, investors expecting prices to continue climbing through 2030 may be mistaken. Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung are set to open and ramp up new production facilities in late 2028.

So, it's likely pricing peaks in 2028 ahead of the massive ramp-up in production capacity. Earnings could peak in late 2028 or early 2029 as a result.

How much should investors pay for Micron's earnings?

Story Continues

Importantly, as supply constraints ease, prices go down, gross margins decline, and operating costs increase. Once supply reaches equilibrium or exceeds demand, profits can sink quickly. And given the massive amounts memory chipmakers are spending on new capacity, the next downcycle could lead to a big drop in earnings.

The potential for that drop will affect how much investors are willing to pay for the stock's earnings near the cycle peak. A bigger drop-off in earnings will result in a lower multiple on the stock. Micron and its competitors are working to reduce the cyclicality of their businesses by signing long-term agreements with customers, but that may only delay an earnings decline and make the drop-off worse once those contracts expire.

As such, investors are unlikely to pay a very high multiple near Micron's peak earnings. Historically, Micron has commanded a multiple of 3-8 times earnings at its peak. With the potential for a large downcycle, shares are likely to trade in the 3-5-times range, with earnings expected to peak in 2028 or 2029.

It's important to note that the stock price usually peaks before earnings peak. Investors are almost always forward-looking. Any hint that pricing is nearing its peak and earnings are set for a near-term downturn will push the stock lower. We saw that happen last month when Sandisk reported disappointing price improvements for its flash memory NAND chips, and the stock dropped after earnings .

With analysts currently expecting $211 per share in earnings for fiscal 2028 and $218 per share for fiscal 2029, that puts my prediction for Micron's stock price at the end of 2028 somewhere between $610 and $1,040. With the stock trading for $690 right now, it doesn't look like a great time to buy unless you think the earnings cycle will last much longer and the drop-off in earnings will be far less severe once earnings peak.
