news.Title: Costco’s U.S. Comparable Sales Jumped 12.6% in October. Here’s the Number That Shows Its Moat Is Widening.
news.Content:
Costco (NASDAQ:COST) is far removed from the artificial intelligence trade, but it's still juicing investor's portfolios. Shares have surged 29% in 2026 (as of Nov. 16), with huge gains coming in the past couple of months. Investors are warming up to the retail stock , perhaps as a safe-haven play in these uncertain times.

The company's strong performance remains the highlight. Costco's comparable sales in the U.S. jumped 12.6% year over year in October (specifically the four weeks that ended Nov. 1). Even excluding impacts from gasoline sales and foreign exchange, this figure rose 8.1%. The growth has proven durable in various economic environments.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Investors that seek high-quality businesses might already have Costco on their radar. Here's the one number that shows the economic moat is widening.

Image source: Getty Images.

Success depends on a steadily expanding member base

At the end of the 2026 fourth fiscal quarter (ended Aug. 30), Costco reported having 84.1 million membership households. That's up 3.8% year over year. And it has risen 36% in the past five years. I believe this single metric underscores the company's moat, as it represents a sticky customer base that brings in recurring membership revenue.

An ever-expanding membership base proves that Costco is delivering an impressive value proposition to more people around the world. This is particularly important in the competitive retail sector. Walmart 's (NASDAQ:WMT) Sam's Club and BJ's Wholesale Club (NYSE:BJ) are direct rivals. Amazon 's (NASDAQ:AMZN) popular Prime membership also can't be ignored.

And even at its huge size, with $24.5 billion in October net revenue and more than 900 warehouses globally, Costco is still able to grow. If the customer base was shrinking, that would be a clear sign of a weakening moat.

A higher membership base also means that Costco's key competitive advantage remains valid. The company's massive scale is critical to its enduring success. The average warehouse sells 4,000 stock-keeping units, well below the 30,000 at typical supermarkets. Costco's significant revenue base means that it's buying enormous volumes from suppliers of fewer goods, which gives it negotiating leverage. These savings get passed on to shoppers.

Story Continues

Inflation is rising more than expected. In these times, when households are focused on getting the most value from their spending, it seems that becoming a Costco member is a no-brainer decision. That mentality drives greater membership sign-ups.

The leadership team is happy with the results. Although consumers remain under pressure, chief executive officer Ron Vachris says Costco is gaining market share.

Pinning down the right valuation for Costco is tricky

Buying an outstanding business doesn't guarantee above-average returns. Investors don't want to overpay. Valuation is the missing link.

Five years ago, this large-cap stock traded at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 46.7. At that time, Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), which was the most valuable company in the world whose shares soared 449% in the prior half decade, sold at a P/E multiple of 26.9. Knowing this, any rational observer would've agreed that Costco was expensive, a stance that would have discouraged owning the leading retailer.

In the last five years, however, the stock price has climbed 114%. It crushed the overall market.

Today, the P/E ratio sits at a steeper 53.5. Again, the consensus view is likely that this presents no margin of safety. In fact, value investors will say that buying now is a risky move, as expectations are high, which introduces more downside risk should Costco miss analyst estimates in any upcoming quarterly financial update.

The stock moved 24% higher in the past two months, after starting at a P/E ratio of 43.1. It's impossible to know what the "right" valuation to pay is when it comes to Costco. I believe this company is uninvestable right now. Paying a big premium to the market, even though the business has staying power, is hard to justify.

news.Title: Nvidia Stock Falls to $150 Per Share. Is It a Buy Now?
news.Content:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has been a huge topic of discussion in the stock market in recent weeks. Former CEO Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia. While he has issued a statement expressing his willingness to return, the Board of Directors has stated that it has no intention of bringing him back at this time. That isn't a pretty situation, but Nvidia is doing quite well right now. Longtime CFO Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement.

The entirety of Q3's results were achieved under Huang's leadership, so there was no question about their impressive nature. What comes next is how the company does without him at the helm. However, there are positive signs there as well.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

With Nvidia stock at about $150 per share, I think it's a generational investment opportunity investors cannot afford to miss.

Image source: Nvidia.

Nvidia is simply an incredible company

During Q3, Nvidia's revenue totaled $116 billion, up around 103% year over year. For a multitrillion-dollar company, increasing revenue by 40% or more is unheard of, let alone doubling it year over year. Nvidia is at the center of all things artificial intelligence (AI), and there are no better-positioned companies to take advantage of the AI build-out than this experienced chip designer.

While some investors may be worried about what happens without Huang, Nvidia's products are basically selling themselves. Last quarter, Nvidia told investors to expect 70% revenue growth in 2027 (fiscal year 2028, ending January 2028). Now, that figure is 75%. There is clearly huge demand for Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs), and whether Huang is at the helm of the Nvidia ship is beside the point.

2027 won't be Nvidia's last year of growth, either. All the language from the AI hyperscalers suggests the build-out could last at least through 2030 . Indeed, Nvidia already projects Q4 revenue of roughly $130 billion as cloud customers lock in multi-year chip supply. The company has a huge runway ahead, and Nvidia's stock should benefit as a result -- if the market values it at its full potential.

Right now, the market is heavily discounting Nvidia's stock because it's unsure of the future. However, if Nvidia can deliver on its promises to investors, the stock is incredibly undervalued.

Story Continues

Nvidia's stock is dirt cheap

Thanks to the sell-off over the past few weeks, Nvidia has reached a valuation previously thought unattainable. It now trades at just 19 times trailing earnings.

NVDA PE Ratio data by YCharts

For reference, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) trades at about 23 times trailing earnings. But that doesn't do Nvidia's stock justice.

The reality is that Nvidia is growing incredibly fast, and valuing the stock based on trailing earnings overlooks huge gains ahead. If Nvidia were growing at a market-average pace, I wouldn't have this same opinion, but because it just doubled its revenue year over year and expects 75% growth next year, valuing the stock based on next year's earnings projections makes a lot of sense.

From this perspective, Nvidia hangs out in Wall Street's bargain bin, trading at an unbelievable 9.4 times next year's earnings.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

It's hard to believe that a company as dominant and successful as Nvidia finds itself at such a low price, but that's where the stock currently stands.

If you think a fair price for Nvidia is around 30 times earnings (which is where most big tech companies trade), Nvidia's stock could more than triple by the end of next fiscal year if it hits targets and reaches that valuation.

Nvidia may be experiencing turmoil in its leadership, but there is plenty to love about the business to warrant investing in the stock today.

news.Title: Bitcoin Has Traded Below Its 200-Week Average Only 8.4% of the Time. History Says This Is When Patient Investors Get Paid.
news.Content:
In typical fashion, Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) is taking investors on a bumpy ride. The world's first and most valuable digital asset has had short spurts of positive momentum this year. But in the past month, the price has tanked 28% (as of Nov. 21), with a five-day drop of 9%.

Bitcoin is currently trading nearly 14% below its 200-week moving average (WMA). According to River, a Bitcoin financial services firm, the leading cryptocurrency has only been in this territory 8.4% of the time in its entire life. It's a rare occurrence, indeed, and it shows that bearish sentiment is ruling the narrative right now.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

History says the bulls should stay patient. This is when investors get paid.

Image source: Getty Images.

A rare signal with a strong track record

The 200 WMA smooths out Bitcoin's wild price swings. It tracks the average closing price over roughly four years, which coincides with the investment community's view of the digital asset's full market cycle. This is why many long-term investors treat it as a baseline.

As of Nov. 21, the 200 WMA sits at $68,130, and Bitcoin is trading about 14% beneath it. According to River, Bitcoin purchased during past periods when it traded below its 200 WMA returned an average of 120% over the following year. The subsequent three-year gain is 582%. At those averages, $10,000 would have grown to $22,000 after 12 months and $68,200 after 36 months.

It all sounds so easy, but investors shouldn't take those figures at face value. Because Bitcoin has rarely traded this low relative to its long-term average, the sample size is small. Many of those episodes came when Bitcoin was a niche experiment a decade or more ago. At a $1.2 trillion market cap, the cryptocurrency is unlikely to compound at the same pace as in its early years. Still, the direction of the pattern is hard to ignore.

The recent drop also needs context. Every past Bitcoin bear market included several rallies of 25% or more. This time is similar. That last surge occurred in the back half of August and September.

However, depth is the noticeable change. So far, this downturn has been much more muted than prior ones. Bitcoin is 53% below its peak now.

There are many takeaways. A smaller fall suggests a more mature asset with steadier holders. It could mean the bottom isn't in yet, and it might leave less upside going forward.

Story Continues

Historical patterns rhyme

Every bear market brings its own reason to declare Bitcoin dead. The past down cycle in 2022 saw major exchange failures that harmed the industry's reputation. Before that, there were worries about government intervention.

Today's fear is more technical in nature. Critics argue that advances in artificial intelligence and quantum computing could break Bitcoin's cryptography. This would undermine the network's security. That's a real concern for any industry in 2026 and beyond.

There's no reason to panic yet. The real threat is likely many years away, and the Bitcoin community, fully aware of how technology is rapidly evolving, can adapt. Network updates can bolster the cryptographic setup over time.

There's also a track record worth noting. The Bitcoin network has operated for over 17 years with virtually no outages. That's a remarkable streak for any piece of financial infrastructure.

The smart money is paying attention. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings show that many of Wall Street's biggest companies added to their Bitcoin positions last quarter. But the leading cryptocurrency probably still accounts for less than 0.1% in most of their clients' portfolios, River says. That's a very tiny percentage among powerful companies with trillions of dollars in assets under management. A modest allocation bump could bring in demand and translate into substantial buying pressure.

Of course, Bitcoin is no sure thing. It's volatile, and past performance offers no guarantees.

That's where dollar-cost averaging comes in. Investors commit a fixed sum at regular intervals, whether the price is up or down. You avoid market timing, and in periods like the current one, a fixed sum gets you more Bitcoin.

Just remember to never invest more than you're willing to lose, and keep your eyes on the long term.

news.Title: AbbVie (ABBV) Stock Just Got a 5.2% Dividend Increase. Here's How Many Shares You Need to Generate $1,000 a Year.
news.Content:
If you're in the market for a healthcare stock for your long-term portfolio, pharmaceutical giant AbbVie (NYSE:ABBV) offers several compelling reasons to invest in.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Here's a closer look at AbbVie and some of those reasons to consider it. First, though, let's talk dividends.

AbbVie stock recently sported a dividend yield of 2.4%. That's quite solid, but it might have been higher had the stock not popped by 28% year to date (as of Nov. 18). (A stock's dividend yield is its total annual dividend amount divided by the stock price, so when the stock price rises, the yield falls, and vice versa.)

Better still, it's a growing dividend. The current $1.82 quarterly payout is up 5.2% from the previous $1.73, and up from $1.41 in 2022 and $0.57 in 2016. And AbbVie has hiked its payout for 53 years in a row , making it a Dividend King.

Let's say you're looking for $1,000 in annual income from AbbVie. How many shares would you need to own? The math is straightforward: The total payout for the year is $1.82 times four, or $7.28 for the year. Divide $1,000 by $7.28, and you'll get the needed number of shares: 137.36.

At a recent stock price of $284 per share, 137 shares will cost you... roughly $39,000.

But would you want to invest in AbbVie? I'm a shareholder myself, but I'd hesitate to jump in right now because the recent valuation seems a bit high. The recent price-to-sales ratio of 7.7, for example, is well above the five-year average of 5.4, and the forward-looking price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 17.6 is also well above the five-year average of 13.9.

So maybe just add it to your watch list, hoping for a lower entry point. Or just start a small position in it now -- as long as you aim to hang on for many years. Its last earnings report was good, with revenue up 10% year over year and immunology drugs Skyrizi and Rinvoq performing particularly well.

news.Title: Got $500? 2 Quantum Computing Stocks to Buy Right Now
news.Content:
Five hundred dollars doesn't stretch very far anymore. It buys a nice pair of headphones, a few weeks of groceries, or one good weekend away. It can also get you a small stake in one of the strangest machines anybody is trying to build.

The idea behind quantum computing is easier to picture than it sounds. A regular computer bit works like a light switch: on or off. A qubit is closer to a dimmer that can sit anywhere in between, and when qubits are linked, they can work together to explore a huge number of possibilities. The problem is that qubits are as fragile as a soufflé. A tiny bit of heat or vibration and the whole thing collapses.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The fix is the "logical qubit," a team of physical qubits that works like a choir. If one singer drifts off key, the others hold the note. Whoever builds lots of reliable logical qubits first wins the race.

Here are two quantum computing companies working on this very issue that I'd be willing to split a $500 investment in.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Infleqtion

Infleqtion (NYSE:INFQ) traps single atoms with lasers and uses them as qubits. In September 2026, it said it had linked 30 logical qubits in a single computation using just 80 physical qubits, hitting its 2026 goal. "Delivering 30 logical qubits is an important step on our technology roadmap," CEO Matt Kinsella said.

Its hardware is already in real machines. Infleqtion's processor powers Shunkai, Japan's first working full-stack neutral-atom quantum computer. "Bringing a full-stack quantum system into production operation is a meaningful step toward fault-tolerant quantum computing," said CTO Pranav Gokhale.

The part I like most is that the same atoms do other jobs today. Infleqtion's Tiqker clock keeps precise time when GPS is jammed, and it recently ran for two weeks straight aboard a U.S. Navy vessel. "The Navy needs dependable timing to navigate, communicate and coordinate operations in the field," Kinsella said. NASA also expanded its quantum gravity sensor contract, and the U.K. funded a compact radio-direction-finding system.

That government work is also its weak spot. Last quarter, it cost Infleqtion more to deliver its work than it earned, partly because of timing on the NASA gravity program and thin margins on a contract that was wrapping up. Spending is climbing fast too. Its operating loss was about five times larger than a year ago. The cash it raised through its special-purpose acquisition company ( SPAC ) merger gives it room for now.

Story Continues

2. Xanadu: Betting the farm on light

Xanadu Quantum Technologies (NASDAQ:XNDU) uses particles of light as qubits. "Our chips compute without coolant," CEO Christian Weedbrook said, and they can be made with the same kind of silicon processes chipmakers already use.

Light's enemy is loss, meaning photons that leak away before the math is done. Weedbrook called it "our most important engineering challenge," but added, "This is primarily a challenge of engineering, not physics." In November, Xanadu and HyperLight cut the loss in a key optical switch by nearly two-thirds.

It's also lining up help. Xanadu signed hardware partnerships with GlobalFoundries (NASDAQ:GFS), ASML (NASDAQ:ASML), and Bluefors, and launched Backline, error-correction software built with Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD). Mitsubishi Chemical used its algorithms to model semiconductor materials, and Royal Bank of Canada and Booz Allen use its software to train staff. Canada is putting about $140 million toward Inception, a Toronto photonics plant Xanadu expects to start using early next year.

Here's the catch: Xanadu barely has revenue, and it's choosing to keep it that way for now. "Pursuing revenue before meaningful quantum utility or selling systems prematurely would ultimately divert talent and resources," Weedbrook said. Its target for a commercially viable machine is 2029 or 2030, and until then, its cash burn keeps rising. Xanadu can also sell more shares through an existing program, and an executive said the company weighs that "almost on a day-by-day basis."

The bottom line on these two quantum stocks

Quantum stocks like these trade on hope as much as results, so I'd treat both like small-cap stocks and size them so a bust stings rather than hurts. I'd put about $300 into Infleqtion, since it's already getting paid for its atoms, and $200 into Xanadu as the long shot. One is earning while it builds. The other is betting everything on getting the light right, and $500 lets you own both stories without needing either one to be perfect.

news.Title: Warren Buffett Successor Greg Abel Piled $28 Billion Into This Stock in the First Half of 2026, But Opted Not to Buy More at a Lower Price Last Quarter
news.Content:
Greg Abel has already started to make his mark on Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRKA) (NYSE:BRKB). The CEO took over the job from Warren Buffett at the start of the year, and he's since gone to work deploying tens of billions of dollars worth of capital for shareholders. He completed the acquisitions of OxyChem and Taylor Morrison Homes for a total of $18 billion. He reinitiated repurchases of the stock, buying back more than $16 billion worth of Berkshire through October. And he's added considerably to Berkshire marketable equity portfolio, including buying an estimated $28 billion worth of Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) stock.

While Abel increased his share repurchases in the third quarter and continued to look for opportunities to fully acquire other companies, he stopped buying Alphabet shares. That's despite the fact that the share price moved meaningfully lower than the price he paid in Alphabet's $10 billion private placement with his company. Investors may be wondering if anything's changed for Alphabet since that purchase and whether it's worth buying right now.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Greg Abel. Image source: The Motley Fool.

Has the thesis on Alphabet changed?

Buffett built Berkshire Hathaway on the ethos of long-term buy-and-hold investing, and Abel has promised to maintain that philosophy in every investment decision he makes for the company. That said, a long-term outlook doesn't mean Buffett hasn't been known to quickly change his mind on a company, especially if things change. Only a handful of marketable equity investments have stuck around for Buffett's preferred holding period of "forever."

Buffett laid out the investment thesis for Alphabet, a position he initiated for Berkshire last year, in an interview this summer. It boils down to the fact that Alphabet has an opportunity to deploy a lot of capital and earn a high return on its invested capital doing so. In other words, Buffett believes Alphabet's massive AI build-out will produce exceptional cash flows over the long run.

While there are growing concerns that Alphabet won't achieve high returns on capital, the financial results so far suggest it's seeing excellent results. Alphabet's Google Cloud segment grew revenue 103% year over year last quarter while expanding its operating margin. That acceleration is tied to a ramp-up in investments starting in 2023, right in line with the timeline of how long it takes before breaking ground on new data center construction translates into placing servers and networking equipment available for rent on its platform.

Story Continues

Alphabet's reported payback period is well above that reported by other hyperscalers. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said it takes about two years for it to generate revenue equal to the cost of the average server for its cloud platform. However, its custom TPU systems have a payback period of half of that. Over time, a greater portion of Alphabet's capital expenditures will go toward revenue-generating servers and a greater share of those servers will be its own custom hardware with faster payback periods.

As such, it makes sense for Alphabet to raise capital and burn cash to build new data centers. The return on invested capital is extremely high and the opportunity is absolutely massive. It's playing out exactly as Buffett expects.

Should you (and Berkshire) buy Alphabet stock?

If Abel liked Alphabet stock at a price of $355 per share, which is what Berkshire paid for the stock in its private placement, he should like it even more at $280 per share, where it trades today.

The stock traded around $340 per share throughout the second half of the third quarter, so there was an opportunity for Abel to add to the position before the quarter ended at a price he was previously comfortable paying. However, Alphabet was already Berkshire's third-largest position as of the end of the third quarter, without any additional shares. That could push the bar higher for Abel to add to the position and increase Berkshire's portfolio concentration. (It's notably why I personally haven't added to my own position in Alphabet amid the pullback, as it already accounts for a significant portion of my portfolio.)

For investors without a significant position in Alphabet, though, right now looks like an incredible buying opportunity for the stock. Shares trade at just 21 times forward earnings expectations, and the long-term growth potential of its cloud computing segment (which includes its TPU system sales) looks better than ever.

Considering the drop in share price pushed Alphabet to become a much smaller portion of Berkshire's portfolio, Abel may be inclined to buy more shares again this quarter after last quarter's pause.

news.Title: Is AMD the Stock to Buy With Nvidia in Limbo?
news.Content:
With all the unknowns surrounding Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) right now, some investors are starting to wonder if Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) is the semiconductor stock to turn to instead. This is a natural progression because the two are competitors in the data center space.

Any analysis of a possible change should start by asking whether AMD is a viable alternative. Does AMD have problems of its own to contend with?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

My analysis suggests there's at least one issue that investors must watch out for, and I think it is definitive in determining which stock is the better pick right now. Let me explain.

Image source: Getty Images.

AMD is delivering solid results

AMD is commonly viewed as an alternative to Nvidia. Nvidia's data center products were more advanced than AMD's when the initial artificial intelligence build-out kicked off, and that allowed Nvidia to seize early market share. First-mover advantage can be difficult to overcome, and with a significant majority of data center computing infrastructure being built for Nvidia products, AMD has found itself in a deep hole.

However, the biggest problem AMD faces isn't hardware; it's software. Nvidia's CUDA software is considered better than AMD's ROCm software, although AMD has improved recently. Still, this is an advantage Nvidia holds over AMD, and it has created a gap unlikely to be closed.

AMD has seen increased success in the data center realm as clients look for cheaper alternatives to Nvidia GPUs, which can be quite expensive due to high demand. During the third quarter, AMD's data center revenue rose 97% year over year to $8.5 billion. However, because AMD also has significant consumer and embedded processor divisions, the results are a bit worse when the entire company is examined. Companywide, AMD's revenue rose 45% year over year to $13.4 billion. Considering that Nvidia is posting $100 billion-plus in quarterly revenue, AMD is a much smaller company.

Normally, being a smaller company is an advantage because it's easier to grow faster. But that hasn't been the case here. Nvidia has outpaced AMD's growth every step of the way, which is impressive considering the fact that it's almost 9 times larger than AMD. I think this speaks to the unbreakable lead that Nvidia has built from a technological and market-share standpoint.

Story Continues

However, with new leadership coming to power at Nvidia, it could shift how the company approaches product development and the market. This could lead to a shifting landscape over the next five years, but as of now, Nvidia remains the leader, with AMD in second place.

That's still not the reason I'm avoiding investing in AMD. AMD has stock problems of its own.

AMD's stock is very pricey

AMD is one of the more expensive stocks in the market right now. If you use next year's earnings projections to value the stock, it trades for about 29 times next year's earnings.

AMD PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

That's a pretty expensive price tag. Not even some of the AI hyperscalers have that expensive a price tag. Furthermore, Nvidia is far cheaper, trading at around 10 times next year's earnings.

While I understand that Nvidia deserves something of a price discount due to leadership uncertainty and the sources of its sales, 10 times next year's earnings is an absolute steal. Nvidia could lose half of its earnings and still trade at less than 20 times next year's earnings.

That's a huge pricing mismatch, and I think that the market has gone too far in discounting Nvidia. As a result, I don't think that AMD is the best stock to buy during Nvidia's turmoil. Instead, Nvidia is likely the best stock to buy , as the market has far overblown what is going on with the stock.

news.Title: Wall Street Asks What Can Save AI Trade After Anthropic Wipeout
news.Content:
(Bloomberg) -- It's been a tough month for the stock market, rocked by back-to-back punches from the stunning ouster of Jensen Huang from Nvidia Corp. and the Democrats' decisive victory in the midterm elections.

Most Read from Bloomberg

Nasdaq 100 Has Worst Week Since 2020 on AI Drama: Markets Wrap

CrowdStrike Is in Talks to Buy Cybersecurity Firm Zscaler

H-1B Visa Workers Are Fed Up and Abandoning American Tech Jobs

Modi Tries to End Trump Photo-Op in Awkward Viral Moment

Anthropic CEO Vacations at Italian Resort After Public Listing

Anthropic PBC's record-breaking initial public offering this week was supposed to provide some relief and change the mood. It didn't. Instead, it raised more questions about the struggling artificial intelligence trade, and tech stocks continued to sell off, led by chipmakers, with Nasdaq 100 Index tumbling 10% for the week, its worst performance since the Covid pandemic hit in March 2020.

Now, with few positive catalysts and a series of obvious risks on the horizon, starting with the Federal Reserve's expected interest-rate hike next month, Wall Street is wondering what will inspire stocks to start climbing again. Instead of finding inspiration to buy, investors just keep discovering reasons to sell, as seemingly every other news headline — from air travel shutdowns to financial hacks — fuels suspicion that technology isn't adapting to the risks posed by AI.

"The market is in limbo-land, especially when it comes to tech and AI," said Paul Nolte, market strategist and senior wealth manager at Murphy & Sylvest Wealth Management. "You need to gird your loins and expect a period of volatility and downside risk."

The Anthropic deal could mark the end of the AI trade, Anna Wong, an economist with Bloomberg Economics, wrote in a report on Thursday. The company's financials show weakening pricing power for frontier intelligence, she wrote, meaning that even with all the demand for AI services, leading providers are having trouble getting customers to pay enough for it to justify their spending.

Of course, in a vacuum, Anthropic's IPO did fine. It was priced over its targeted range, and when combined with a separate private placement of shares, the company raised the most cash for a new issue ever, topping SpaceX's deal in June. The stock even raced higher out of the gate. But it quickly plateaued and then started retreating. By the end of Friday it was less than $6 from where it went public.

The bigger issue is it ushered in more selling rather than giving investors a reason to buy. By the end of Friday, the Nasdaq 100 was teetering on the brink of bear market, defined as a 20% decline from a recent high, while the S&P 500 Index had entered a correction after falling 12% from its October record.

Story Continues

Skeptical Times

All that selling laid bare the magnitude of the questions swirling around AI more than four years into a bull market powered by huge bets on the technology.

"There was a hope that the Anthropic IPO would provide a sustained boost, but the trading there is indicative of the broader concerns surrounding AI," said Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisors. "Anthropic came to market at a time of more general skepticism surrounding the space, and there are a lot of questions about their ability in the near term to deliver on increasingly lofty expectations."

Democratic victories in the midterms raised the risk that data center construction will slow since many of the party's candidates ran on blocking their development. Meanwhile, the risk of higher interest rates raises the cost of capital as big data center developers increasingly turn to credit markets for funding.

"A lot of the growth in AI is dependent on how and whether companies can fund their capital needs," said Malcolm Polley, director of strategic market analysis at Stratos Investment Management, which has $3.6 billion in assets. "Will they need to fund that through capital or debt markets? Until we know the cost of capital, we can't adequately value the asset, and if the cost of capital is going higher, then valuations need to come down."

But it's the chaos at Nvidia that really has spooked investors. The company ousted Huang on Nov. 12 after he admitted having an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, and the stock has been in a tailspin ever since. Even a strong earnings report featuring a raised revenue forecast for next fiscal year and a $150 billion stock buyback authorization couldn't stop the selling, as the question remained who will be Huang's permanent replacement.

Nvidia shares plunged 23% this week, their worst performance since 2008. The stock is down 48% from an Oct. 6 all-time high.

The turmoil appeared to create openings for Nvidia's competitors, including chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc. But that bet took a hit on Thursday when a short seller raised questions about AMD's business in China, which could be hurt by more US chip export restrictions. The shares plunged 20% in the final two sessions of the week.

More broadly, it's the sustainability of the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent to expand computing power that's driving the selloff. That spending has juiced earnings for companies across the AI ecosystem, from chipmakers and networking gear manufacturers to electricity providers and industrial companies. But investors are increasingly skeptical that it can last.

Chip Stocks Swing

This rapid swing from greed to fear is best seen in the trading of semiconductor stocks this year. Chips are historically a cyclical business, rising with demand and then falling as it dissipates. But the belief was that this history would be rewritten as years of AI demand would break the cycle. The Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index more than doubled in the first half of the year on that bet. But it has lost 41% in the second half as investors rethink those positions.

Memory and storage stocks, which also are major beneficiaries of the AI spending, have been among the hardest hit over the last few months. Sandisk Corp. was leading the S&P 500 in the first six months of year, soaring 857%. It's the worst stock in the index in the second half, dropping 72%. Western Digital Corp. has tumbled more than 65% from a June record, while Micron Technology Inc. is down more than 50% from its all-time high.

Of course, some optimism remains on Wall Street. In particular the hope is the selloff is nearing exhaustion as investors have used the opportunity to reduce risk, according to Brian Smedley, chief investment officer and head of Cynosure Strategies, the hedge fund division of the Cynosure Group.

"I think investors will gain confidence that AI demand remains exceptionally strong, and that the key players — Anthropic among them — will continue to have very healthy growth prospects," he said. "The market has overshot to the downside, just as it overshot to the upside earlier this year."

One thing investors agree on is that Anthropic's debut will provide a new level of visibility into the business of selling AI services.

"It has been hard to get a real feel for AI demand, and Anthropic is the answer to that question," said Marta Norton, chief investment strategist at Empower. "We will know more about the upside of AI, in terms of demand and the return, at the same time that we will be getting a reinforced view of how crazy wildly expensive it is."

In the meantime, strategists are advising clients to stay nimble.

"It's hard to say what it might take to catalyze gains after this week," said Mark Luschini, chief market strategist at Janney Montgomery Scott. "I want to see whether this selloff metastasizes into something more severe. We're oversold, but not deeply so. We could plumb lower still. I want to see stabilization before I make a strong commitment."

news.Title: Nvidia stock extends $2.7 trillion rout as SEC probe reportedly investigates its accounting
news.Content:
Nvidia's worst week on record just got worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books.

Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock fell 14% Friday, its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss, before bouncing nearly 4% in after-hours trading. The drop came as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting issues.

The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment.

The selling set records. Nvidia shed about $490 billion in market value Friday and nearly $900 billion this week, as its stock had its worst week since October 2008. That tops the $573 billion it lost last week, previously the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ).

Nvidia's latest quarterly report raised a few questions. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.

Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China.

Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on.

Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO. President Trump said Friday he "would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," while criticizing the chipmaker's new leadership .

California is digging in too. Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia Thursday, investigating whether its advanced chips reached China and whether the company misled investors. "Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said.

Story Continues

The sell-off spread across chip stocks , which had their worst week since 2001 , and the broader market.

Baird's Ted Mortonson, a technology desk sector strategist, saw more scrutiny coming even before Friday's report.

"Every single deal that Nvidia has done on circular finance is going to be put under the microscope," he said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.

news.Title: Jensen Huang's next move: Wall Street floats Intel and SpaceX, but bettors are banking on a surprise second act
news.Content:
F. Scott Fitzgerald wrote that there are no second acts in American lives. Silicon Valley has spent 40 years proving him wrong.

Jensen Huang has been out as Nvidia's ( NVDA ) CEO for barely a week, and everyone already has a script for him. President Donald Trump, who has defended Huang from the start, would prefer a rerun. "I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said at a White House briefing Friday , adding that a smart Nvidia would accept Huang's apology and let him return.

The casting call comes in one of the worst weeks for tech stocks in years. Nvidia has lost more than $2.7 trillion in market value since its Oct. 6 record high, nearly $900 billion of it this week, as an SEC probe reportedly looks into its accounting. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) closed in a correction Friday, and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) lost 10% for the week.

Wall Street has its own scripts. Speculation from Mizuho cites Huang as leading Intel's ( INTC ) AI chip strategy, though no talks have been reported. Asked on X about hiring Huang, Elon Musk replied , "That would be an honor."

Musk has also said he's signing a petition to reinstate Huang at Nvidia, along with Uber founder Travis Kalanick, who staged a second act of his own after Uber pushed him out in 2017.

The people putting money on it are backing neither. On Polymarket , the top pick for Huang's next formal role is a company he starts himself, at 27%, ahead of no new job before 2028, at 24%. A return to Nvidia gets 20%, SpaceX 8%, and Intel 3%, in a small market with about $64,000 traded.

History has a part for every script

Steve Jobs lost his operating role at Apple ( AAPL ) in May 1985 and started NeXT about four months later. Apple bought NeXT 11 years after that, and Jobs came with it. Musk was pushed out as PayPal's CEO in 2000 and founded SpaceX ( SPCX ) about 18 months later, so the company floated for Huang is itself a second act.

Intel would cast Huang as Lee Iacocca. Henry Ford II fired Iacocca as president of Ford ( F ) in 1978, and within four months, he was running the struggling Chrysler, which was later rescued by federal loan guarantees. Washington has owned roughly 10% of Intel since August 2025. But Huang is still Nvidia's largest individual shareholder, with a stake worth about $102 billion at Friday's close.

Scandal isn't always career-ending

Mark Hurd left HP ( HPQ ) in August 2010 after an expense-report probe tied to a personal relationship, and Oracle ( ORCL ) made him co-president a month later. Oracle stock rose about 6% the next session, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Larry Ellison had called Hurd's ouster "the worst personnel decision since the idiots on the Apple board fired Steve Jobs many years ago."

Story Continues

Don't expect Huang's sequel soon. He faces a closed-door House interview Dec. 1 and has agreed to testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee. California's attorney general subpoenaed Nvidia Friday, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday he wants "answers in the next 10 days" from Nvidia's board. Bettors give Huang about a 4% chance of joining a new company this year.

news.Title: Quantum-Proof Accounts Are Coming to the XRP Blockchain by 2028. That's Not Likely to Be a Game Changer for XRP.
news.Content:
According to Ripple, the creator of XRP (CRYPTO:XRP), the XRP Ledger (XRPL) will have quantum-secure wallets by 2028. Ripple itself set that target date in April of this year, and the XRP Ledger Foundation officially placed the corresponding upgrade onto its roadmap on Nov. 4.

XRP could sure use a catalyst, with its price being down 73% from its all-time high set in July 2025. But making more secure wallets will probably not do what holders are hoping for regarding the coin's price, at least not outside a very narrow and improbable set of circumstances. Here's why this upgrade probably won't be a game changer.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

This change is meant to counter a distant and uncertain threat

First, let's get some clarity on what is even at stake with the issue of security against quantum computers.

In technical terms, each XRP wallet, like nearly all other crypto wallets, has a secret private key and also a public key that anyone can see on a wallet-scanning website. The private key is what grants access to move funds from the account.

Deriving the private key from the public one is impossible in practical terms with today's hardware. But a powerful enough quantum computer could theoretically do exactly that in the future, meaning an attacker with such a computer could steal funds from individual wallets and likely spark a mass exodus of capital once the theft was discovered.

In March of this year, Alphabet 's Google researchers published a paper estimating that breaking the cryptography that secures most crypto wallets could be possible with a significantly weaker quantum computer than previously expected. In a survey published in March 2026, the Global Risk Institute found that experts put the odds of such a machine arriving within 10 years at 28% to 49%.

Therefore, the XRPL's target preparedness date of 2028 probably leaves it with a decent margin of error if quantum computers advance faster than anticipated due to quantum computing companies ramping up their efforts.

Plus, given that quantum computers are massive, complex systems, the first dangerous machines will probably belong to governments and the largest companies building them, not ordinary hackers. However, an owner of such a machine may not announce it.

Story Continues

How this could benefit XRP's price

The direct impact of XRPL wallets becoming quantum-secure on its price will almost certainly be minimal.

The upgrade will not increase demand for the coin on its own. And while financial institutions might find it appealing that the XRPL is quantum-secure in advance, it's unclear whether they're willing to pay anything for it.

However, adapting early could pay out big in one specific future scenario .

If a powerful enough quantum computer becomes widely available years before most cryptocurrencies have implemented security measures and it's successfully used to carry out a major crypto hack, capital might flee to XRP as a safe haven.

But don't hold your breath for that to happen; even if the XRPL is an early mover in this domain, there are many other quantum-secure blockchains already in existence, and likely more to come.

news.Title: Nvidia Just Issued a Major Warning to AMD and Intel Stock Investors
news.Content:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) released solid results for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 (which ended on Oct. 25) on Nov. 17 and backed its outstanding performance with impressive guidance.

Its data center business recorded healthy growth once again last quarter, and Nvidia's upgraded guidance for fiscal 2028 suggests that the segment will continue to move the needle substantially next year. However, a closer look at Nvidia's results suggests it is quickly gaining ground in a market where Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) are the dominant players.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Let's take a closer look at this particular business and check why Nvidia's progress in this space doesn't bode well for Intel and AMD.

Image source: Nvidia.

Nvidia's Vera CPUs are in terrific demand

The market for server central processing units (CPUs) has been growing rapidly amid the increasing adoption of agentic AI and inference applications. This explains why Nvidia decided earlier this year to offer its latest-generation Vera server CPUs as a stand-alone product to customers.

The company already had a server CPU before Vera, known as Grace, but it was available as part of rack-scale systems that integrated graphics cards, networking chips, memory, and other components into a single package. Nvidia's latest quarterly report is proof that its move into the stand-alone server CPU market is paying off.

The product has been adopted by leading hyperscalers, neocloud providers, and AI companies, including Oracle , Meta Platforms , OpenAI , CoreWeave , Nebius , and others. In fact, Nvidia has doubled down on the server CPU market by offering a CPU-based rack-scale server platform to handle agentic AI and inference applications.

Interim CEO Colette Kress remarked on the latest earnings call:

We continue to see very strong demand for Vera and expect total CPU revenue to more than double in fiscal year 2028.

Though the company didn't specify exactly how much revenue it generated from stand-alone sales of the Vera CPU last quarter, it noted on the fiscal Q1 earnings call that it expects $20 billion in revenue from this product in fiscal 2027. Assuming the estimate is still intact, Nvidia's Vera VPU revenue could jump to at least $40 billion next fiscal year.

This should set the alarm bells ringing for AMD and Nvidia investors.

Story Continues

AMD and Intel's fast-growing server CPU business could be under threat

At its Financial Analyst Day held in November last year, AMD predicted that the data center CPU market will be worth $26 billion. The company's 2030 server CPU estimate was $60 billion a year ago, suggesting a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 18% for the next five years.

However, AMD has significantly upgraded its 2030 server CPU estimate. It noted earlier this year that the server CPU market could generate $220 billion in revenue in 2030, clocking a CAGR of more than 50%. The good part is that AMD is making the most of this opportunity. It expects server CPU revenue to more than double in 2027.

On the other hand, Intel's data center and AI (DCAI) revenue increased by 78% year over year in Q3 to $7.3 billion, driven by record demand for its Xeon server CPUs. Intel expects server CPU shipments to increase by 30% in 2026 and 2027. These numbers from Intel and AMD suggest that Nvidia is quickly becoming more influential on their turf, which is a big deal considering that it entered the stand-alone server CPU market just this year.

We have already seen that AMD anticipates server CPU market revenue to grow at a 50% CAGR through 2030. Nvidia is already growing at double the pace of this market, giving tough competition to AMD. Intel, however, could be the bigger loser from Nvidia's entry into server CPUs, as the latter is already forecasting significantly stronger growth in this market.

So, even though Nvidia has fallen out of favor on Wall Street lately, its strong growth indicates it is a solid buy right now, especially given its attractive valuation relative to peers.

NVDA PE Ratio data by YCharts

Notably, Nvidia has increased its fiscal 2028 revenue growth forecast to 75% from the earlier expectation of 70%, citing growing demand for its chips, including the Vera CPU. The healthy revenue growth will translate into a robust increase in earnings per share as well.

NVDA EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

So, Nvidia looks like the best bet among these three semiconductor stocks right now, as its terrific earnings growth potential and attractive valuation are poised to drive further stock price upside.

news.Title: Social Security's Trump Bump-Led 2027 COLA Is the 5th Largest in 35 Years -- but There's a Dark Side to This Outsize Increase as Well
news.Content: For Social Security's nearly 72 million traditional beneficiaries -- retired workers, workers with disabilities, and survivors of deceased workers -- there are few, if any, announcements more anticipated than the annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA). Social Security's COLA is the near-annual "raise" given to beneficiaries to account for inflation (i.e., rising prices). If the price for the goods and services that seniors regularly purchase kept climbing without an adjustment in benefits, the buying power of Social Security income would steadily decline over time. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Social Security's announced 2027 COLA offers something of a mixed bag for recipients. On the one hand, it's set to deliver one of the largest raises over the last 35 years. This larger payout comes courtesy of President Donald Trump and a handful of his policies. President Trump's policies offer a good-news/bad-news scenario for Social Security. Image source: Official White House Photo by Molly Riley. But this outsize Trump bump isn't without its consequences . Larger payouts in the new year can make the program's precarious financial outlook that much worse. One of the largest payout increases since 1993 is on the way On Oct. 14, the Social Security Administration announced that monthly payouts would increase by 3.6% in 2027. For the average retired-worker beneficiary, their monthly payout is expected to climb by $75. Meanwhile, the typical worker with a disability can expect their monthly Social Security check to rise by $59 in the new year. A 3.6% raise is well above the norm. It marks a tie for the fifth-largest percentage increase over the last 35 years, surpassed only by COLAs of 4.1% (2006), 5.8% (2009), 5.9% (2022), and 8.7% (2023). It's also the sixth consecutive year in which recipients have received at least a 2.5% cost-of-living adjustment. It's been 30 years (1988-1997) since benefits rose by at least 2.5% for six straight years. While modest inflation associated with a growing U.S. economy results in a Social Security raise most years, next year's outsize COLA was pumped up by two of President Donald Trump's policies. To begin with, each of the last two Social Security COLAs has been influenced by Trump's tariff and trade policy. Adding duties to imports directly raises their price and can increase manufacturing costs for domestic producers. Story Continues A recently published report by three New York Federal Reserve economists writing for Liberty Street Economics ("How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through into Consumer Prices?") found that Trump's 2025 tariffs increased goods price inflation by an estimated 2.9 percentage points by February 2026. Without tariffs, the NY Fed economists estimate that goods prices would have otherwise fallen. The other major policy contributing to Social Security's 2027 Trump bump is the Iran war. Closing the Strait of Hormuz has resulted in the largest energy supply disruption in modern history, sending gas and diesel prices notably higher. With Trumpflation (inflation driven by Trump's policies) becoming entrenched in the U.S. economy, it's quite possible that these policies provide a third consecutive year with a Trump bump in 2028. Image source: Getty Images. Big Social Security raises come with even bigger question marks about the program's solvency Unfortunately, outsize Social Security COLAs come at a potentially steep cost to America's leading retirement program. Every year since 1985, the Social Security Board of Trustees Report has warned of a long-term unfunded obligation. In simpler terms, the projected income to be collected in the 75 years following the release of a report is expected to be insufficient to cover outlays (primarily benefits, but also the administrative costs to oversee Social Security). As of 2026, this long-term unfunded obligation had ballooned to $29.3 trillion. However, this isn't the most pressing concern for the program or its nearly 72 million traditional beneficiaries. According to the latest Trustees Report, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund (OASI) is forecast to exhaust its asset reserves by the fourth quarter of 2032. The OASI's asset reserves represent the excess income collected since inception that is invested in special-issue, interest-bearing government bonds, as required by law. US Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund Assets at End of Year data by YCharts. The positive news is that Social Security isn't going bankrupt and is in no danger of halting benefits. More than 91% of the program's income is collected through the 12.4% payroll tax on earned income (wages and salaries, but not investment income). As long as Americans keep working, the payroll tax will continue generating income for disbursement to eligible beneficiaries... even if the OASI's asset reserves are depleted. But just because Social Security isn't going bankrupt, it doesn't mean everything is peachy. If the OASI's asset reserves run dry over the next six years, as predicted, it would indicate that the current payout schedule, inclusive of annual COLAs, isn't sustainable. Sweeping benefit cuts of up to 22% may be necessary for retired workers and survivors of deceased workers. The concern is that Social Security's Trump bump may have materially altered the trajectory to the OASI's asset reserve insolvency. When the Trustees Report issues its short- and long-term outlooks, it takes into account a long list of variables, including birth rates, death rates, net migration rates, and even annual COLAs. The Trustees assume that annual COLAs will be modest -- but as we just saw, a 3.6% annual raise is anything but average. Social Security's outsize 2027 raise risks draining the OASI even faster than initially forecast. President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill" already moved up the projected OASI asset reserve insolvency timeline by one quarter (from the first quarter of 2033 to the fourth quarter of 2032). It's entirely possible the 2027 Trump bump further accelerates the timeline to sweeping benefit cuts. But a handful of little-known "Social Security secrets" could help ensure a boost in your retirement income. For example: one easy trick could pay you as much as $23,760 more ... each year! Once you learn how to maximize your Social Security benefits, we think you could retire confidently with the peace of mind we're all after. Many Americans leave money on the table in retirement. news.Title: If AI Chips Become Commoditized, Nvidia Has the Most to Lose, While These 3 Stocks Are Set to Gain
news.Content:
The AI chip market is starting to shift, and with it, Nvidia 's (NASDAQ:NVDA) grip. Anthropic recently revealed that its Claude Mythos model could start running part of its AI models on alternative AI chips to Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) in just a few days with basically no human intervention, a process that used to take six to 12 months and dozens of engineers. This greatly reduces Nvidia's CUDA moat at a time when competitors are starting to catch up.

Alphabet 's (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) have started to outperform Nvidia's GPUs on a performance-per-dollar basis, according to Semianalysis (though some dispute the results). Meanwhile, Advanced Micro Devices ' (NASDAQ:AMD) GPUs continue to gain traction. The company has improved its software stack, and its chips' larger memory capacity makes them ideal for inference.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

If the gap between AI chips continues to shrink and AI models can be quickly shifted to run on any AI accelerator, this is very bad news for Nvidia. Not only will the company continue to lose market share, but, more importantly, its pricing power will erode, and its margins will shrink. The Nvidia premium can be seen in its gross margins , which are in the mid-70% range, versus AMD's in the mid-50% range. Meanwhile, all of Nvidia's largest customers, outside of SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), have been developing their own custom AI chips to try to break free of Nvidia's high prices.

All is not lost for Nvidia, as the company still holds some advantages. It has created a cohesive hardware, software, and networking ecosystem that should still be able to command a premium. It also has major current supply chain advantages, having locked up more access to constrained high bandwidth memory (HBM) supply and having more manufacturing and packaging capacity with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM). That will help it maintain its leadership position, even as it will likely face continued market-share and pricing pressure.

While Nvidia may struggle, these three AI stocks look set to benefit.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing

Lower AI accelerator prices and more Nvidia GPU alternatives could boost overall AI chip demand, which would benefit Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing. It would also lower TSMC's customer concentration and could actually help with pricing power and gross margins.

Story Continues

Whether a hyperscaler, neocloud, enterprise, or government buys Nvidia GPUs, AMD accelerators, or ASICs through a company like Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) or Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL), TSMC still wins at the end of the day. That makes the stock a buy.

Alphabet

As both a cloud computing giant and a developer of TPUs, Alphabet is one of the best-positioned companies to benefit from the commoditization of AI chips. Alphabet has more than a decade's head start with custom chips and is creating an ecosystem to rival chipmakers like Nvidia and AMD. This lets it get better utilization out of its data centers and gives it an advantage over other companies using their own custom AI chips.

Meanwhile, because its offerings cost much less than Nvidia's, it should be able to gain share with external customers without sacrificing margins. This ultimately could make Alphabet one of the biggest winners in the AI space during this transition.

Starting from a much smaller market-share base with an operating model already built around slimmer gross margins, AMD should benefit as AI chips become more commoditized. Between its lower prices, improving cost performance, and the recent introduction of a complete AI rack system (Helios), AI chip pricing normalization and chip fungibility actually become a tailwind rather than a headwind for a smaller Nvidia competitor like AMD.

Meanwhile, the market is heading in AMD's direction with inference and agentic AI, with customers caring far more about memory capacity, central processing unit (CPU) integrations, and cost-per-action, which is where its chips shine. With its new Helios system, which combines its GPUs and CPUs, AMD has a big opportunity to establish itself as a meaningful alternative to Nvidia in the coming years. This makes the stock a buy.

news.Title: IonQ vs. Alphabet: Which is the Better Quantum Computing Stock to Own for Next 5 Years?
news.Content:
While AI gets all the headlines, quantum computing is starting to become a technology that's becoming more and more interesting. Several companies are making strides in quantum computing endeavors, and the technology is only years away from being commercially viable.

The big question investors must answer in this space is whether it's best to go with a massive company that has huge resources that can make a successful quantum computer, or if it's better to back a pure-play company that is much smaller.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Two of the most popular options in this segment are Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and IonQ (NYSE:IONQ), with Alphabet being the giant and IonQ the smaller player. It's the classic David versus Goliath matchup, but which one makes the most sense? It all depends on your risk tolerance.

Image source: Getty Images.

IonQ is making huge strides

When comparing Alphabet's and IonQ's quantum computing technologies, it is a bit difficult to draw direct comparisons. IonQ releases information about every breakthrough it makes and keeps the investing public well informed of its progress. Alphabet is more silent, although it does release updates about its quantum successes from time to time.

At the surface level, some may think that Alphabet is being silent because it's behind and doesn't want to publicly display that information, but I don't think that's what's going on.

IonQ doesn't have a business to fund its operations. It must find partners and raise capital to continue its operations. Unless IonQ can show these entities that it's making progress and that its technology is coming along nicely, it won't be able to drum up enough interest to keep its company going.

On the flip side, Alphabet is self-funding its quantum research. It only has to keep internal leaders happy with progress, and staying under the radar is a smart idea on their part. So, it's natural that Alphabet doesn't release as many updates as IonQ.

But that doesn't mean IonQ is behind by any means.

Next year, it's releasing its Superion 256-qubit quantum computer. With IonQ's backlog rising to $1.2 billion, it has generated a lot of interest. While this machine isn't quite ready for commercial-level workloads, it's a step in the right direction, and several clients are ordering the machine so they can start to develop quantum computing programs for future implementation. Depending on how this launch goes, it could vault IonQ into a leadership position. It also has plans to build a 10,000-qubit computer, which would be the first commercial-level computer ready for purchase. That's still a few years out, but with quantum technology progressing rapidly, it will be here before investors know it.

Story Continues

But does that make it a better buy than Alphabet for a quantum-focused investment?

IonQ isn't for everyone

IonQ isn't a stock that everyone should own. In fact, I would argue that most shouldn't. Why? Its chance of success is low. While Alphabet hasn't been public with its quantum computing products, the reality is that its products are competitive with IonQ and boast similar fidelity. Alphabet isn't the only big tech company , either. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and IBM (NYSE:IBM) are also heavily investing and represent well-funded competition to IonQ.

If IonQ works out, it will be a huge winner. But there's high risk involved because if it loses to any of its peers or the big tech companies, the stock could plummet to $0. IonQ is a high-risk, high-reward investment. If investors want exposure to quantum computing without the risk of extreme failure, then Alphabet makes for a great stock pick . If you're OK with more risk in exchange for upside, then IonQ is a smart option. Just be sure to size the position appropriately to account for the risk.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again

In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you'd invested $5,000 then, you'd be sitting on $1,897,590 today.*

Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It's a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast.

Continue »

*Stock Advisor returns as of November 21, 2026.

news.Title: Prediction: Here’s Where Alphabet Stock Will Be in 5 Years
news.Content:
There's a lot of concern over what the future holds for Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL). The internet company has transformed from an asset-light business into an extremely asset-heavy business, as it and its hyperscaler peers are set to spend trillions of dollars building new data centers for artificial intelligence over the next few years.

That shift has led to a significant sell-off in the stock. Shares are down 30% from their peak in late spring. The biggest culprit is Alphabet's negative free cash flow in each of the last two quarters, as well as management's commentary suggesting cash burn could push even deeper into the red next year.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

With the stock trading at just 21 times forward earnings, the market isn't expressing much faith that the business will produce meaningful returns on its invested capital. That's despite financial results and management commentary suggesting it could quickly see a cash-flow turnaround and head much higher. Here's my prediction for where Alphabet stock trades in five years.

Image source: Getty Images.

A huge investment cycle could pay off massively

Alphabet plans to spend between $195 billion and $205 billion on capital expenditures this year. CFO Anat Ashkenazi also said she expects capex "to increase significantly in 2027."

Analysts expect Alphabet's cash burn to peak in 2027. For the full year, Alphabet could spend $80 billion more in cash than it brings in. 2028 could see it burn through another $50 billion. But free cash flow could turn positive again in 2029.

Importantly, Alphabet ended the third quarter with $56 billion in cash and about $209 billion in marketable equities. That puts it on strong financial footing and gives it multiple ways to fund the continued build-out of its AI data centers: It can use its cash, sell its marketable equities (once lock-ups expire), sell more debt, or raise cash via its own equity.

All that cash is going toward building new data centers (which have a useful life of 40 years) and outfitting them with servers and networking equipment (which have a useful life of six years). About 65% of spending is currently going toward the latter this year.

Over time, however, a much higher percentage should go toward revenue-generating servers, reducing the business's capital intensity and enabling it to generate strong free cash flow .

Story Continues

The results are already showing up in Alphabet's cloud computing segment. The steep ramp-up in spending that started in 2023 has led to accelerating Google Cloud revenue growth. That includes revenue growth exceeding 100% in the most recent quarter, indicating the delay between spending and revenue generation. But the payback period on Alphabet's spending is getting shorter.

Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian says its payback period for the average server on Google Cloud Platform is about two years. But the payback period for its own Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) systems is less than half of that. With a useful life of six years and the amount Alphabet is spending on servers, the cash-generating ability of these investments over the useful life is absolutely massive.

Alphabet's Cash flow is set to explode by the end of the decade

With a further step-up in spending in 2026 and 2027, investors should expect continued growth in Google Cloud revenue in 2028 and 2029. Beyond those years, more stable spending should result in significant cash generation. In fact, analysts currently expect Alphabet's free cash flow, excluding stock-based compensation, to reach $305 billion by 2031.

With that level of free cash flow generation, Alphabet stock should be worth significantly more than it is today. Prior to the start of the investment cycle in 2023, Alphabet shares traded around 30 times free cash flow. If it can recover that multiple in 2031 while generating $300 billion in free cash flow (less than analysts currently expect), it'll be worth $9 trillion total.

Considering the stock currently sports a market cap of less than $3.5 trillion, that could be a fantastic return for shareholders over the next five years. It's even a safe bet if you expect management to dilute shareholders by issuing more equity to raise capital over the next few years. But more than likely, it'll offset that dilution with massive buybacks in the outer years once it starts printing hundreds of billions of cash.
